mainTopic: פדיון שבויים as a מצוה רבה, and the rules and praise of community charity (קופה, תמחוי, and גבאי צדקה)
overview: The עמוד opens by saying that פדיון שבויים, freeing captives, is a great מצוה. רבה בר מרי proves this from a פסוק in ירמיהו that lists four punishments, and רבי יוחנן explains that each one is worse than the one before it. Captivity comes last, so it is the worst, because it includes all the others. Next, a ברייתא gives the rules of the town's two charities. The קופה (money fund) is collected by two people and given out by three, for the town's poor. The תמחוי (daily food) is collected and given out by three, for any poor person. The town may switch the funds, and it may also set prices and wages. The גמרא explains why two collectors are needed: it is because of authority, not trust. Collectors may even force a wealthy person to give. After words of praise for judges, collectors, teachers and Sages, more ברייתות teach how collectors must avoid any suspicion. The עמוד ends with אביי's stories about how רבה changed his charity practices, and the second story continues on the next עמוד.

steps.title: Redeeming captives is a great מצוה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that פדיון שבויים is a מצוה רבה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Redeeming captives is a great מצוה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wraps up the earlier discussion by stating that freeing captives is a great מצוה. This sets up the next question, which asks where that idea comes from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This line ends what came just before it on the דף. It gives us the rule: פדיון שבויים is not just any מצוה but a 'great' one. The next step will ask for the source of this claim.

keyTerms.meaning: Redeeming captives: paying to free people taken prisoner
A great מצוה, an especially important one

phrases.english: Redeeming captives is a great מצוה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the earlier discussion on the daf that leads into this section.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: פדיון שבויים has the status of a מצוה רבה.

steps.title: רבא asks for the source
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks רבה בר מרי where we learn that פדיון שבויים is a great מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רבה בר מרי: Where do we get this idea the Rabbis said, that redeeming captives is a great מצוה?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks for the source of the rule we just heard. He is setting up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא is not doubting the rule. He wants to know which פסוק or reason shows that freeing captives is more important than other מצוות.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַבָּה בַּר מָרִי:
phrases.english: Rava said to Rabba bar Mari:
From where is this matter that the Rabbis said
that redeeming captives is a great מצוה?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the rule stated in step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for calling פדיון שבויים a מצוה רבה.

steps.title: The verse listing four punishments
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר מרי answers with a פסוק in ירמיהו that lists death, sword, famine, and captivity.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: As it is written: 'And when they say to you, where shall we go? You shall tell them: So says ה׳: those for death, to death; those for the sword, to the sword; those for famine, to famine; those for captivity, to captivity.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר מרי quotes a פסוק that lists four punishments in a set order. This is the first half of his answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By itself, the פסוק only lists the four punishments, with captivity last. The key point is the order, which the next step explains.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is written (introduces a פסוק)

phrases.english: He said to him: As it is written:
"And it shall be, when they say to you: To where shall we go?
Then you shall tell them: So says the Lord:
Those for death, to death;
and those for the sword, to the sword;
and those for famine, to famine;
and those for captivity, to captivity."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering רבא's question with a פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The source is the פסוק in ירמיהו 15:2, which lists captivity last.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: each one is worse than the one before
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן teaches that every punishment listed later in the פסוק is harsher than the one before it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: Whatever comes later in this verse is harsher than the one before it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן explains how to read the order of the פסוק: it goes from lighter to heavier.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since captivity comes last, it is the worst punishment. So freeing someone from captivity saves them from the worst fate, which is why it is a great מצוה. The גמרא will now prove each step of the ranking.

keyTerms.meaning: Harsher than its fellow (the one before it)

steps.whyThisMatters: This principle turns a simple list into the proof: captivity, the last item, is the harshest, so redeeming captives is a מצוה רבה.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל הַמְאוּחָר בְּפָסוּק זֶה קָשֶׁה מֵחֲבֵירוֹ.
phrases.english: Whatever comes later in this verse is harsher than the one before it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer by explaining what the order of the פסוק teaches.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In ירמיהו 15:2, each punishment is harsher than the one listed before it.

steps.title: Sword is worse than death: the logical reason
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says sword is worse than natural death, offers either a פסוק or סברא as proof, and gives the סברא first: the sword disfigures the body.
steps.simpleTranslation: Sword is harsher than death. If you want, say a verse; if you want, say a logical reason. The logical reason: this one (the sword) disfigures the body, and that one (natural death) does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins proving רבי יוחנן's ranking, starting with sword versus death. It says there are two possible proofs and gives the logical one first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Death' in the פסוק means an ordinary, natural death. Being killed by a sword is worse because the body is damaged and disgraced. The proof from a פסוק comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say: introduces one of two possible proofs

phrases.english: Sword is harsher than death:
If you want, say a verse;
and if you want, say a logical reason.
If you want, say a logical reason:
This one is disfigured,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is a person killed by the sword.

phrases.english: and that one is not disfigured.
phrases.notes: 'That one' is a person who dies a natural death.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts proving the first link in רבי יוחנן's ranking.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sword is worse than natural death, because it disfigures the body.

steps.title: Sword is worse than death: the verse
steps.stepSummary: The proof from a פסוק: 'Precious in the eyes of ה׳ is the death of His pious ones.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say a verse: 'Precious in the eyes of ה׳ is the death of His pious ones.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the second proof, from a פסוק in תהלים, that sword is worse than death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק calls the death of the pious 'precious,' which suggests that a plain death is a dignified way to leave the world. A violent death by sword does not have that quality.

phrases.english: And if you want, say a verse:
"Precious in the eyes of the Lord is the death of His pious ones."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the second, verse-based proof promised in step 5.
steps.raayaObject: That sword is worse than natural death.

steps.title: Famine is worse than sword: the logical reason
steps.stepSummary: Famine is worse than the sword, because the starving person suffers and the one killed by sword does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Famine is harsher than sword. If you want, say a logical reason: this one (famine) suffers, and that one (sword) does not suffer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next link in the ranking, famine versus sword, and starts with the logical reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person dying of hunger suffers slowly for a long time. A sword death is quick. That long suffering makes famine harsher.

phrases.english: Famine is harsher than sword:
If you want, say a logical reason:

phrases.aramaic: הַאי קָא מִצְטַעַר, וְהַאי לָא קָא מִצְטַעַר.
phrases.english: This one suffers, and that one does not suffer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proves the second link in רבי יוחנן's ranking, in the same pattern as step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Famine is worse than the sword, because of the drawn-out suffering.

steps.title: Famine is worse than sword: the verse
steps.stepSummary: The proof from a פסוק in איכה: 'Better off were those killed by the sword than those killed by famine.'
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say a verse: 'Better off were the victims of the sword than the victims of famine.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the verse-based proof that famine is worse than the sword.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the פסוק says it outright: those killed by the sword were better off than those who died of hunger.

phrases.english: If you want, say a verse:
"Better off were the victims of the sword than the victims of famine."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the verse-based proof for the claim in step 7.
steps.raayaObject: That famine is worse than the sword.

steps.title: Captivity is the worst, because it includes them all
steps.stepSummary: Captivity is harsher than all the others, because a captive can face death, sword, and famine.
steps.simpleTranslation: Captivity is harsher than all of them, because all of them are found in it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the ranking: captivity is the worst punishment. This completes the answer to רבא's question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A captive is at the mercy of the captors and can suffer every one of the other three punishments. So captivity sits at the top of the list. Freeing a captive therefore rescues a person from the worst of all fates.
steps.whatToRemember: פדיון שבויים is a מצוה רבה because, according to the order in ירמיהו 15:2 as explained by רבי יוחנן, captivity is the harshest punishment: it is worse than famine, which is worse than the sword, which is worse than death, and it includes all of them.

phrases.english: Captivity is harsher than all of them,
phrases.notes: The words in square brackets are part of the corrected wording; either way, the meaning is the same.

phrases.english: because all of them are found in it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ranking and so finishes the answer to רבא's question in step 2.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Captivity includes every other punishment, so it is the worst, and redeeming captives is a great מצוה.

steps.title: The charity fund: collected by two, given out by three
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that the קופה של צדקה is collected by two people and distributed by three, and gives a reason for each number.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: The charity fund is collected by two people and given out by three. It is collected by two because we don't put authority over the public in the hands of fewer than two people. It is given out by three, like a court for money cases.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by quoting a ברייתא about the town charity fund. It says how many people collect it and how many hand it out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Collecting means having power over the public, and that power should never sit with just one person, so two are needed. Giving out the money means deciding who gets what, which is like judging a money case. That is why three are needed, like a בית דין for דיני ממונות.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
The charity fund is collected by two,
and distributed by three.
It is collected by two —
because one does not appoint authority over the community
of fewer than two,
and it is distributed by three — like monetary cases.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: קוּפָּה שֶׁל צְדָקָה נִגְבֵּית בִּשְׁנַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new section on charity rules after the discussion of which punishment is worst.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The קופה is collected by two people because public authority needs at least two, and it is distributed by three people, like דיני ממונות.

steps.title: The food platter: collected by three and given out by three
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: the תמחוי is collected and distributed by three, because its collection and distribution happen together. It also says how often each one runs.
steps.simpleTranslation: The food platter is collected by three and given out by three, because collecting it and giving it out happen at the same time. The platter runs every day; the fund runs from one Friday to the next.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא moves on to the second kind of charity, the daily food platter. It explains why three people collect it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תמחוי is collected and given out on the same day. So the three people who will hand it out also do the collecting. The קופה is only handed out once a week, on ערב שבת, so two people can collect it and a third can join them later for the distribution.

keyTerms.meaning: Charity food platter, collected and given out daily

phrases.english: The charity platter is collected by three,
and distributed by three;
because its collection and its distribution are the same.
phrases.notes: He means they happen on the same day, so the people handing it out are already there collecting.

phrases.english: The platter — every day,
the fund — from Shabbat eve to Shabbat eve.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא, comparing the תמחוי to the קופה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The תמחוי needs three people for both collecting and distributing because both happen together every day. The קופה is distributed weekly.

steps.title: Who each charity serves, and the town's right to switch them
steps.stepSummary: The תמחוי serves any poor person; the קופה serves the town's own poor. The townspeople may move funds between them and use them however they want.
steps.simpleTranslation: The platter is for the poor of the world; the fund is for the poor of the town. The townspeople may turn fund money into platter food and platter food into fund money, and change its use to whatever they want.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives one more difference between the two charities, who gets them. Then it says the town is allowed to switch them around.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תמחוי feeds anyone who comes through town, while the קופה supports the local poor. Even so, these are not fixed rules the town is stuck with. בני העיר may move money from one to the other, or change its purpose, based on what the community needs.

keyTerms.meaning: Poor people from anywhere, including travelers

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read 'poor of the world' versus 'poor of the town' as an unbreakable law. The same ברייתא right away lets the town switch the funds.

phrases.english: The platter — for the poor of the world,
the fund — for the poor of the town.
And the residents of the town are permitted to make
the fund into the platter, and the platter into the fund,
and to change it to whatever they want.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּמְחוּי – לַעֲנִיֵּי עוֹלָם, קוּפָּה – לַעֲנִיֵּי הָעִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds who each charity serves and gives the town power to switch funds.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The תמחוי is for all poor and the קופה for local poor, but בני העיר may switch the funds and change their purpose as they see fit.

steps.title: The town may set measures, prices and wages, and fine violators
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא ends by giving בני העיר the power to set measures, prices and workers' wages, and to fine people who break those rules.
steps.simpleTranslation: The townspeople may also make rules about measures, prices and workers' wages, and fine people who break their rules.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes by widening the town's power beyond charity. The town can make rules for the local market and enforce them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just as the town may decide how charity is used, it may also set binding rules for business: measures, prices and wages. It may also back up these rules with fines. This finishes the ברייתא that the גמרא will go on to discuss.

keyTerms.meaning: To set terms, make binding rules
To fine those who break their set rules

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא: the קופה is collected by 2 and given out by 3 every Friday, for the town's poor. The תמחוי is collected and given out by 3 every day, for all poor. The town may switch them, and may also set measures, prices and wages, with fines.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a key source for the power of a community to make binding local rules and enforce them.

phrases.aramaic: וְרַשָּׁאִין בְּנֵי הָעִיר לְהַתְנוֹת עַל הַמִּדּוֹת,
phrases.english: And the residents of the town are permitted to set terms for the measures,
and for the prices, and for the wages of workers;
and to fine people for breaking what they set.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַשָּׁאִין בְּנֵי הָעִיר לְהַתְנוֹת עַל הַמִּדּוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Widens the town's power from charity to market rules, and ends the ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בני העיר may set measures, prices and wages, and may fine anyone who breaks these rules.

steps.title: Where do we learn that authority needs at least two people?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא's rule that community authority needs at least two people and asks for its source.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: You may not set up authority over the community with fewer than two people. Where do we learn this from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to a line from the ברייתא about charity collection and asks for its source. It is setting up the next move, which will be a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 10 said the קופה is collected by two people. Here the גמרא names the reason behind that rule: one person alone may not hold authority over the צבור. Now it wants to know where that rule comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: "The Master said": the way the גמרא quotes back a line from a ברייתא it already brought
"From where are these words?": asking for the source of a rule

phrases.english: The Master said:
phrases.notes: This quotes back the ברייתא about the charity fund from a few steps ago.

phrases.english: One does not set up positions of authority over the community
with fewer than two people.
From where do we know these words?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to a line inside the ברייתא and asks for its source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural source for requiring at least two people in community authority.

steps.title: The source is the plural 'they' in the משכן verse
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן brings the פסוק about the people who took the gold for the משכן. It says "they," which means more than one person.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: The verse says, "And they shall take the gold, etc."
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן answers the question with a פסוק about the people who received the donations for the משכן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says "they" will take the gold, not "he." So the people handling the community's donations were a group of at least two. That becomes the model for any authority over the צבור.

keyTerms.meaning: "The verse says": introduces a פסוק as a proof
"Etc.": the rest of the פסוק continues (written וגו׳)

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said:
The verse says:
"And they shall take the gold, etc."
phrases.notes: שמות 28:5. The key word is "they": more than one person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the source question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The plural "they" in the פסוק about taking the gold for the משכן shows that such a role needs at least two people.

steps.title: The rule is about authority, not about trust
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא infers that two collectors are needed because of authority. A single person would still be trusted with the money.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is authority that is not given to one person. But as for trusting him with money, one person is trusted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads the wording of the ברייתא closely and draws an inference from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא spoke about "authority," not honesty. So the need for two people is not because we suspect one person might steal. One person alone is trusted with the money. He just should not hold power over the community by himself.

keyTerms.meaning: Trustworthiness with money (being a trusted keeper)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think two collectors are needed because one might steal. The גמרא says the opposite: one person is fully trusted. The pair is needed only because of the power involved.

phrases.english: It is authority that they do not give to one person,
but when it comes to trust, he is trusted.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׂרָרוֹת הוּא דְּלָא עָבְדִי, הָא הֵימוֹנֵי מְהֵימַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from the wording of the rule that was just sourced.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two collectors are needed because of authority. A single person is trusted with money.

steps.title: This supports רבי חנינא's story of two brothers
steps.stepSummary: The inference supports רבי חנינא, who reported that רבי once appointed two brothers over the charity fund.
steps.simpleTranslation: This supports רבי חנינא, for רבי חנינא said: Once רבי appointed two brothers over the charity fund.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the inference from the last step fits a known story told by רבי חנינא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If two collectors were needed so that each could watch the other, two brothers would be a poor choice. But since one person is already trusted, two brothers are fine. The second person is only there because of authority, so רבי's appointment makes sense.

keyTerms.meaning: "This supports him": a source backs up someone's view

phrases.english: This supports Rabbi Chanina,
for Rabbi Chanina said:
There was an incident, and Rebbi appointed
two brothers over the charity fund.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the inference agrees with רבי חנינא's report.
steps.raayaObject: The inference that one person alone is trusted with charity money, so two collectors are needed only because of authority.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי חנינא's report that רבי appointed two brothers over the קופה.

steps.title: What authority does a charity collector have?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what power is involved in collecting charity.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the authority?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question to set up the next step: why is collecting charity counted as having authority?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Collecting money from willing givers does not sound like power over anyone. So the גמרא wants to know what makes the collector's job an act of authority.

phrases.english: What is the authority?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what the "authority" from the previous steps actually means.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What power a charity collector holds over the community.

steps.title: Collectors may take collateral to force giving
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן in the name of רבה בר אבוה explains that collectors may take a משכון to make people give צדקה, even on ערב שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב נחמן said in the name of רבה בר אבוה: Because they may take collateral for charity, even on ערב שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: a charity collector can force people to pay by taking their belongings as collateral.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is real power. The collector can take a person's property until he pays his share of צדקה. He can do this even on ערב שבת, a busy and pressured time. That is why the job counts as authority.

keyTerms.meaning: They take collateral (a משכון) to force payment

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ:
phrases.english: As Rav Nachman said in the name of Rabbah bar Avuh:
Because they take collateral for charity,
and even on Erev Shabbos.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers what the authority is.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Collectors may take a משכון to force people to give צדקה, even on ערב שבת.

steps.title: But a פסוק says God will punish charity collectors
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges this using a פסוק about punishing oppressors. רב taught that this includes גבאי צדקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But it is written, "And I will punish all his oppressors," and רבי יצחק בר שמואל בר מרתא said in the name of רב: even charity collectors!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the last answer. If collectors are allowed to force people, why does רב list them among the oppressors God will punish?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 19 said forcing people to give is allowed. רב's teaching treats collectors who push people as oppressors who deserve punishment. These two teachings seem to contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: "But it is written": brings a פסוק as a challenge

phrases.english: Is that so?
But it is written:
"And I will punish all his oppressors,"

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק בַּר שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר מָרְתָא
phrases.english: and Rabbi Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta said
in the name of Rav:
even on charity collectors!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rule that collectors may force payment.
steps.kashyaTarget: The teaching of רב נחמן in the name of רבה בר אבוה that collectors may take a משכון for צדקה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב counts גבאי צדקה among the oppressors God will punish, so forcing people should not be allowed.

steps.title: Force is allowed against the wealthy, not against others
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that collectors may force a wealthy person. Forcing someone who is not wealthy is oppression.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This is when he is wealthy; that is when he is not wealthy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the contradiction by saying each teaching is about a different kind of giver.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן's rule about taking a משכון applies to a wealthy person who can afford to give. רב's warning applies to collectors who press a person who is not wealthy. That is real oppression.

keyTerms.meaning: "It is not difficult": opens an answer that settles a contradiction
Wealthy, someone known to have money
"This ... that": splits two teachings into two different cases

steps.whatToRemember: Charity collectors hold real authority. They may force a wealthy person to give, even by taking a משכון. Pressing someone who is not wealthy makes them oppressors.

phrases.english: It is not difficult;
this is where he is wealthy,
phrases.notes: "This" is רב נחמן's rule allowing a משכון.

phrases.english: that is where he is not wealthy.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא; הָא דַּאֲמִיד, הָא דְּלָא אֲמִיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by splitting the cases.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): wealthy vs. not wealthy
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Forcing anyone to give צדקה would always count as oppression.
steps.terutzMaskana: Forcing a wealthy person is allowed. Forcing a person who is not wealthy is oppression.

steps.title: רבא forced רב נתן בר אמי to give 400 זוז
steps.stepSummary: A story shows the rule in action: רבא forced the wealthy רב נתן בר אמי to give four hundred זוז to צדקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Like the case where רבא forced רב נתן בר אמי and took four hundred זוז from him for charity.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a real story that matches the answer it just gave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נתן בר אמי was wealthy, so רבא was allowed to force him to give. Taking four hundred זוז shows that this power was really used, and on a large sum.

keyTerms.meaning: "Like this case": introduces a story that illustrates a rule

phrases.english: Like that case where Rava forced
Rav Natan bar Ami,
and took from him
four hundred zuz for charity.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דְּרָבָא אַכְפְּיֵהּ לְרַב נָתָן בַּר אַמֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates the answer with a real story.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that collectors may force a wealthy person to give צדקה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבא forcing רב נתן בר אמי to give 400 זוז.

steps.title: A פסוק praising judges and צדקה collectors
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains a פסוק in דניאל. The 'wise who shine like the sky' are honest judges, and 'those who make the many righteous' are גבאי צדקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: "And the wise will shine like the brightness of the sky, etc." "The wise will shine like the brightness of the sky" means a judge who judges a completely true judgment. "And those who make the many righteous, like the stars forever and ever" means the charity collectors.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא has been discussing גבאי צדקה. Now it turns from הלכה to praise, using a פסוק to show how great these collectors are.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק has two halves and the גמרא assigns each half to a different group. The honest judge is the 'wise' one. The גבאי צדקה are those who 'make the many righteous', because they help many people do the מצוה of giving צדקה.

keyTerms.meaning: A judgment that is completely and truly correct
Those who bring the many to righteousness

phrases.english: "And the wise will shine like the brightness of the sky, etc."
"The wise will shine like the brightness of the sky":
this is a judge who judges
a judgment that is completely true.
"And those who make the many righteous, like the stars forever and ever":
these are the charity collectors.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the story of רבא forcing a rich man to give צדקה, the גמרא moves to aggadic praise of the people who collect it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An honest judge is like the shining sky, and גבאי צדקה are like the stars forever.

steps.title: A ברייתא reads the same פסוק differently
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא puts both judges and גבאי צדקה in the first half of the פסוק, and reads the second half as being about teachers of young children.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: "And the wise will shine like the brightness of the sky" means a judge who judges a completely true judgment, and also charity collectors. "And those who make the many righteous, like the stars forever and ever" means those who teach young children.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second explanation of the same פסוק, from a ברייתא. Here the 'stars' are teachers of young children.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The change is in who gets which half. In this version the גבאי צדקה move up into the first half together with the judges. The second half, 'making the many righteous', now goes to teachers, who bring many children to Torah and good deeds.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: It was taught in a ברייתא:
"And the wise will shine like the brightness of the sky":

phrases.aramaic: זֶה דַּיָּין שֶׁדָּן דִּין אֱמֶת לַאֲמִתּוֹ,
phrases.english: this is a judge who judges a completely true judgment,
and also charity collectors.
"And those who make the many righteous, like the stars forever and ever":
these are teachers of young children.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different reading of the same פסוק explained in step 23.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Judges and גבאי צדקה are like the sky, and teachers of young children are like the stars.

steps.title: Which teachers deserve this praise?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what kind of teacher is meant, since not every teacher earns such high praise.
steps.simpleTranslation: Like whom?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for an example of the kind of teacher the ברייתא is praising. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Comparing someone to the eternal stars is huge praise. So the גמרא wants to know what level of dedication a teacher needs to deserve it.

phrases.english: Like whom?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a clear example of the 'teachers of young children' mentioned in step 24.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What kind of teacher is described as being like the stars forever?

steps.title: רב names רב שמואל בר שילת
steps.stepSummary: רב answers that the model teacher is someone like רב שמואל בר שילת.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: Like רב שמואל בר שילת.
steps.whatsHappening: רב gives a real person as the example of a teacher who deserves the praise of the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of a general definition, רב points to a specific teacher. The next step tells a story explaining why he was chosen.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא famous as a dedicated teacher of children

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב: כְּגוֹן רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר שִׁילַת.
phrases.english: רב said: For example, רב שמואל בר שילת.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: כְּגוֹן רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר שִׁילַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 25.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A teacher like רב שמואל בר שילת.

steps.title: The teacher who had not seen his garden in thirteen years
steps.stepSummary: רב found רב שמואל בר שילת in a garden and asked if he had left his students. He answered that he had not seen the garden in thirteen years, and even now his mind was on his students.
steps.simpleTranslation: For רב found רב שמואל בר שילת standing in a garden. He said to him: Have you abandoned your post? He answered him: It has been thirteen years that I have not seen this garden, and even now my thoughts are on them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that shows why רב שמואל בר שילת is the model teacher.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב worried that the teacher had left the children he was responsible for. The answer shows the opposite: he had not taken a break in thirteen years, and even during this short visit he was still thinking about his students.

keyTerms.meaning: Your trust, the job you were trusted with

steps.whatToRemember: A teacher who is fully devoted to his students, even in his thoughts, is like the stars forever.

phrases.aramaic: דְּרַב אַשְׁכְּחֵיהּ לְרַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר שִׁילַת
phrases.english: For רב found רב שמואל בר שילת
standing in a garden.
He said to him: Have you abandoned your trust?
phrases.notes: רב means: did you leave the children you were trusted to teach?

phrases.english: He said to him: It has been thirteen years
that it has not seen me,
phrases.notes: Literally 'it has not seen me', meaning he had not been to this garden in thirteen years.

phrases.english: and even now my mind is on them.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּרַב אַשְׁכְּחֵיהּ לְרַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר שִׁילַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב's choice in step 26 with a story about that teacher's dedication.
steps.raayaObject: That רב שמואל בר שילת is the model of a teacher who deserves the praise of the פסוק.
steps.raayaSupportSource: Story of רב finding him in the garden.

steps.title: What praise is there for the Sages?
steps.stepSummary: After praising judges, collectors and teachers, the גמרא asks what is said about the רבנן, the Torah scholars.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the Sages, what is said about them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks which פסוק describes the greatness of תלמידי חכמים. This sets up רבינא's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in דניאל was already used for other groups. So the גמרא looks for a separate source that praises the Sages themselves.

keyTerms.meaning: And the Sages, what about them?

phrases.english: And the Sages, what about them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of praises from steps 23 and 24 by asking about the Sages.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which פסוק describes the reward of the Sages?

steps.title: רבינא: the Sages are like the rising sun
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers with a פסוק: those who love ה׳ are like the sun coming out in its strength.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: "And those who love Him are like the sun when it comes out in its might."
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא gives the פסוק that describes the Sages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Sages are compared to the sun, which is even brighter than the sky and the stars used for the other groups. Their love of ה׳ is shown through Torah study.

keyTerms.meaning: And those who love Him are like the sun coming out in its strength

phrases.english: רבינא said:
"And those who love Him are like the sun when it comes out in its might."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 28 and closes the aggadic section.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The Sages are like the sun coming out in its strength.

steps.title: צדקה collectors must collect together
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that גבאי צדקה may not split up while collecting. They may separate a little, one to a doorway and one to a store, while staying near each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: Charity collectors are not allowed to separate from each other. But one may go to a gate and the other to a store.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the practical הלכות of collecting צדקה, quoting a ברייתא about how collectors must work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Collectors work as a pair and should not each go off alone. A small split, like one at a house gate and one at a nearby store, is allowed because they are still close by.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught in a ברייתא

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא does not forbid every separation. It forbids going off fully alone, but allows a small split while staying near each other.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
Charity collectors are not permitted
to separate from one another,
but one may separate, this one to a gate
and that one to a store.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: גַּבָּאֵי צְדָקָה אֵינָן רַשָּׁאִין לִפְרוֹשׁ זֶה מִזֶּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the aggadic praise and returns to the הלכות of collecting צדקה from steps 18-22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Charity collectors may not split up fully, but may separate a little, one to a gate and one to a store.

steps.title: Found money goes into the צדקה purse first
steps.stepSummary: If a collector finds coins in the market, he should not put them in his own pocket. He puts them in the צדקה purse and takes them out at home.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he found coins in the market, he should not put them into his pocket. Instead he puts them into the charity purse, and when he comes home he takes them.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with a rule about how a collector handles money that is really his own while he is collecting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The found coins belong to him, yet he may not put them in his pocket in public. People watching might think he is taking צדקה money for himself. So he puts them in the charity purse and takes them back privately at home.
steps.whyThisMatters: A person handling public money must avoid even the appearance of wrongdoing, not only actual wrongdoing.

phrases.english: If he found coins in the market,
he should not put them into his own pocket;

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא נוֹתְנָן לְתוֹךְ אַרְנָקִי שֶׁל צְדָקָה,
phrases.english: rather, he puts them into the charity purse,
and when he comes home, he takes them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with another rule of conduct for collectors.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A collector who finds money puts it in the charity purse in public and takes it out at home.

steps.title: A loan repaid in the market follows the same rule
steps.stepSummary: If someone repays a collector a personal loan in the market, the collector also puts it in the צדקה purse and takes it out at home.
steps.simpleTranslation: Similarly, if someone owed him a מנה and repaid him in the market, he should not put it into his pocket. Instead he puts it into the charity purse, and when he comes home he takes it.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds a second case that works the same way as found money: repayment of a personal loan.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is his own money, and some people may even have seen the repayment. Still, onlookers might not know, so the same careful practice applies. This ends the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: A sum of one hundred דינרים

steps.whatToRemember: גבאי צדקה must collect in pairs and never put money into their own pocket while collecting, even money that is truly theirs, so that no one suspects them.

phrases.english: Similarly,
if another person owed him a מנה,
and repaid him in the market,
he should not put it into his own pocket,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא נוֹתְנָן לְתוֹךְ אַרְנָקִי שֶׁל צְדָקָה,
phrases.english: rather, he puts it into the charity purse,
and when he comes home, he takes it.

steps.triggerLanguage: כַּיּוֹצֵא בּוֹ, הָיָה נוֹשֶׁה בַּחֲבֵירוֹ מָנֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the rule of step 31 to a second case, repayment of a loan.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A loan repaid to a collector in the market also goes into the charity purse first and is taken out at home.

steps.title: Collectors may exchange charity coins with others, not with themselves
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that גבאי צדקה with no poor people to give to may exchange the coins with other people, but not with their own money.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: Charity collectors who have no poor people to give to may exchange the coins with other people, but they may not exchange them with themselves.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about collectors who are holding money but have no one to give it to yet. They may change the coins, but only with someone else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Changing the coins is allowed, so the money itself is not the problem. The problem is the collector doing it with his own money, because people might suspect he gave himself a good deal. This matches the earlier steps, where collectors must avoid even looking like they take charity money.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages taught; this introduces a ברייתא
to themselves, using their own money

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
Charity collectors who do not have
poor people to distribute to
may exchange the coins with others,
but they may not exchange them with themselves.
phrases.notes: He means using their own money for the exchange, which could look suspicious.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: גַּבָּאֵי צְדָקָה שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם עֲנִיִּים לְחַלֵּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another rule to the list of how collectors avoid suspicion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Collectors may exchange idle charity coins with others, but not with themselves.

steps.title: Food collectors may sell extra food to others, not to themselves
steps.stepSummary: Collectors for the תמחוי who have no poor people to feed may sell the food to others, but not to themselves.
steps.simpleTranslation: Collectors for the food platter who have no poor people to give to may sell the food to others, but they may not sell it to themselves.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives the same rule for food collectors. Extra food may be sold, but the collector may not buy it himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The food could spoil, so selling it is allowed. Buying it himself could look like he set a low price for his own benefit. This is the same idea as the coin rule, applied to food.

keyTerms.meaning: the charity food platter, a public fund that gives out food

phrases.english: Collectors for the food platter
who have no poor people to distribute to
may sell it to others
but they may not sell it to themselves.

steps.triggerLanguage: גַּבָּאֵי תַמְחוּי שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם עֲנִיִּים לְחַלֵּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallel rule: the coin rule applied to food collectors.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Food collectors may sell extra food to others, but not to themselves.

steps.title: Charity coins are counted one by one
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא ends by ruling that charity coins are counted one at a time, not two at a time.
steps.simpleTranslation: Charity coins are not counted two at a time, but one at a time.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives one last rule for collectors: count the money slowly, one coin at a time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Counting two at a time is faster but makes mistakes easier. With public charity money, a wrong count could cost the poor or make the collector look dishonest.
steps.whatToRemember: In handling צדקה, collectors must stay clear of suspicion: they work in pairs, keep charity money apart from their own, never deal with themselves, and count carefully.

phrases.english: Coins of charity
are not counted two at a time,
but rather one by one.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָעוֹת שֶׁל צְדָקָה – אֵין מוֹנִין אוֹתָן שְׁתַּיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Final rule of the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Charity coins must be counted one at a time.

steps.title: רבה began sitting on the synagogue mats after hearing a ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: אביי reports that רבה at first would not sit on synagogue mats bought with צדקה money. After he heard a ברייתא that the town may change charity money to any purpose, he sat on them.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: At first, my teacher would not sit on the mats of the synagogue. Once he heard the ברייתא that says the townspeople may 'change it for whatever they want,' he would sit on them.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי tells a story about his teacher רבה. רבה changed his practice once he learned that the town may use charity money for other things.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה worried that the mats belonged to the poor, so using them would be taking from צדקה. The ברייתא taught that the townspeople may redirect charity funds to other uses. So the mats were properly the community's, and sitting on them was allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: the Master; here, אביי's teacher רבה

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the town has the power to decide how charity money is used. That idea leads into the next story about the two purses.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
At first, the Master would not sit
phrases.notes: The Master here is רבה, אביי's teacher.

phrases.english: on the mats of the synagogue.
phrases.notes: These mats had been bought with צדקה money.

phrases.english: Once he heard that which was taught in a ברייתא:
"and to change it for whatever they want,"
he would sit.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: מֵרֵישׁ לָא הֲוָה יָתֵיב מָר אַצִּיפֵּי דְּבֵי כְנִישְׁתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the first ברייתא (step 12) and shows its line about changing charity funds 'to whatever they want' put into practice by רבה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Since the town may redirect charity funds, a person may use community items bought with צדקה money.

steps.title: רבה's two charity purses and שמואל's advice to use one
steps.stepSummary: אביי reports that רבה at first kept two purses, one for poor people from elsewhere and one for the poor of his town. Then he heard that שמואל told רב תחליפא בר אבדימי to make only one purse. The statement continues past this section.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: At first, my teacher made two purses, one for the poor of the world and one for the poor of the town. Once he heard what שמואל told רב תחליפא בר אבדימי, 'Make one purse,'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי starts a second story about רבה. This one is about keeping separate charity purses, and it is setting up שמואל's advice, which finishes in the next part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה kept the two groups' money apart so each group got only what was meant for it. שמואל's instruction to use one purse suggests a single fund is enough. The full reason comes in the continuation of his words.

keyTerms.meaning: the poor of the world, meaning poor travelers from elsewhere

steps.confusionAlert: The sentence is not finished here. שמואל's words and the end of the story continue on the next עמוד, so don't decide yet what רבה ended up doing.

phrases.english: Abaye said:

phrases.aramaic: מֵרֵישׁ הֲוָה עָבֵיד מָר תְּרֵי כִיסֵי –
phrases.english: At first, the Master would make two purses
one for the poor of the world,
and one for the poor of the town.
Once he heard this,

phrases.aramaic: דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ שְׁמוּאֵל לְרַב תַּחְלִיפָא בַּר אַבְדִּימִי:
phrases.english: which Shmuel said to Rav Tachalifa bar Avdimi:
"Make one purse,"

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: מֵרֵישׁ הֲוָה עָבֵיד מָר תְּרֵי כִיסֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story from אביי in the same pattern: רבה changes his practice after hearing a source.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Being set up: שמואל's advice to keep only one charity purse, which is finished on the next עמוד.
